analysis.one_liner: Caps credit card interest at 10% for five years.

how_it_helps.text: Caps child care costs at no more than 7% of household income for participating families
Makes all income-eligible children entitled to assistance rather than limiting slots
Funds universal preschool grants for three-to-five-year-olds in low- and moderate-income families
Expands Head Start to full-day, full-year service and raises teacher pay to a living wage
Appropriates $20 billion in FY2022 rising to $40 billion by FY2024 for child care
Requires provider wages comparable to elementary educators and at least a living wage, with funds to pay for it
Guarantees no copays for families under 75% of state median income
Includes special support for children with disabilities, homeless children, and children in foster care

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, mostly higher-income households, fund the roughly $20–40 billion annual appropriation; no industry pays directly, but providers face new wage floors and quality standards

drawbacks.text: The bill does not identify a funding source; the multi-billion-dollar annual appropriation adds to federal deficits unless offset elsewhere
Setting provider wages comparable to elementary teachers raises operating costs; small providers and family-care operators may struggle to meet the new quality-tier requirements

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill directly attacks a major household cost — child care — for low- and middle-income families, and unlike many subsidy programs it funds the higher wages it requires of providers. The main honest objection is fiscal: it is an expensive open-ended entitlement with no dedicated revenue in the bill itself, and its quality mandates could squeeze small providers even as overall funding grows.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in April 2021 and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it, so it died at the end of the 117th Congress in January 2023 without ever coming to a vote

narrative.text: Senator Murray introduced the bill with 36 of 48 Senate Democrats as cosponsors on April 22, 2021
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, its only action
The bill never received a committee markup, floor vote, or House companion action before the 117th Congress ended

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No family got cheaper child care from this bill. Large national child care chains and current providers keep the existing market in place, and the federal government avoids the roughly $20–40 billion annual cost of a new entitlement. Working parents who spend heavily on child care are the direct losers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Existing child care providers and deficit-focused opponents

for.name: Sen. Patty Murray
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 36 Democratic cosponsors

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral, never scheduling a markup or vote

against.name: 50 of 50 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, leaving it without the support needed to advance in a 50-50 Senate

sides.party_line_note: All 36 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill died in a Democratic-controlled Senate committee without a vote.

industries.note: Providers would gain paying customers and higher reimbursement rates tied to actual costs, plus funds to raise staff wages. In exchange they would face new quality-tier standards and wage floors that could burden small operators.
The bill requires wages comparable to elementary educators and at least a living wage, and funds training, scholarships, and apprenticeships for the workforce.
Agencies would get grants to expand to full-day, full-year service and to raise staff pay to a living wage.
